analysis.one_liner: Strengthens workplace sexual-harassment remedies and expands protections, penalties, and services for victims of sexual and domestic violence.
analysis.headline: A Republican-backed bill to toughen remedies for sexual harassment and violence against women was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let victims of workplace sexual harassment recover monetary penalties of up to $100,000 against an employer for a first offense and $150,000 for repeat offenses, and would have let them get fast court orders stopping the harassment without waiting for the usual agency process. It would have required colleges to report campus sexual assaults to students and parents, extended employment-discrimination law to Congress itself, expanded legal protections against discrimination in contracts and seniority systems, and created new federal penalties and services for sexual and domestic violence, including shelter funds, rape-prevention grants, and full enforcement of protective orders across state lines. It also created a Glass Ceiling Commission to study barriers to promoting women and minorities into executive jobs, and expanded apprenticeship outreach to women. The bill was sent to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Women workers facing sexual harassment would gain a real monetary remedy and fast court relief. Victims of sexual assault, rape, and domestic violence would gain campus crime reporting, state-run rape prevention and education grants, rural and general domestic violence shelter funding, cross-state enforcement of protective orders, and government-paid HIV testing and counseling after an assault. Women and minorities seeking skilled trades apprenticeships and executive careers would gain outreach programs and a study commission. Members of the bill's targets also include crime victims generally through expanded restitution for medical costs, lost income, and related expenses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women workers, assault victims, and college students

how_it_helps.text: Victims of sexual harassment could win monetary penalties of up to $100,000 for an employer's first intentional offense and $150,000 for each later one, addressing findings that existing law often left them with no compensation for medical and psychological harm [S2][S3].

Harassment plaintiffs could seek temporary court orders to stop the harassment immediately, without waiting for the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission process or a right-to-sue letter, and courts would have to expedite these cases [S2][S3].

Title VII's employment-discrimination protections would apply to Congress itself for the first time, and federal civil rights protections against discrimination in contracts would extend to the performance, breach, and termination of contracts, not just their making [S2][S3].

Colleges would have to collect and disclose statistics on rape, sexual assault, and other abusive sexual conduct on campus, and report them to students, parents or guardians, and local police [S2][S3].

States would receive $25 million per year in rape prevention and education grants, with at least 15 percent targeted at junior high and high school students, and states would have to pay the full cost of forensic medical exams for assault victims [S2][S3].

Domestic violence shelter and assistance funding would be expanded, with at least 60 percent directed to shelters and related services and at least 20 percent to rural areas, plus new public-awareness campaign grants and state domestic violence commissions [S2][S3].
Protective orders issued in one state would have to be enforced in every other state, closing a gap that left victims unprotected after moving or traveling [S2][S3].
Sex crime victims could recover restitution for medical and psychological care, rehabilitation, lost income, disease-related costs, and child care and transportation related to prosecution [S3].

A Glass Ceiling Commission would study and recommend ways to remove barriers to advancing women and minorities into executive management, and the Labor Department would fund outreach and preapprenticeship training for women and minorities in registered apprenticeship programs [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear new monetary penalties and injunction costs for workplace harassment, though small employers would get government technical assistance on compliance. Producers, distributors, exhibitors, and sellers of sexually explicit material would face civil lawsuits from victims of sex crimes allegedly incited by the material. States would pay for forensic exams of assault victims, and taxpayers would fund the grant programs, task force, and commission — roughly $25 million per year for rape prevention alone, plus domestic violence, apprenticeship, and EEOC assistance funding. Criminal defendants would face expanded death penalty exposure, doubled sentences for repeat offenses, and broader admissibility of prior-offense evidence.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, adult media sellers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The Pornography Victims' Compensation Act subtitle would let crime victims sue producers, distributors, and sellers of sexually explicit material as proximate causes of a third party's violent crime, on a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard — a theory courts would likely test hard against First Amendment protections for non-obscene speech, and one that could chill lawful expression far from the violent material the findings target [S2][S3].

The bill would make murder in the course of a sex offense or by a repeat sex offender a death-penalty-eligible Class A felony, and would double maximum sentences for repeat federal sex offenders — provisions that expand capital punishment and incarceration rather than prevention, and that civil liberties opponents typically contest [S2][S3].

New federal evidence rules would let prosecutors admit a defendant's prior sexual assault or child molestation offenses in sexual assault and child molestation trials, weakening the usual rule against character evidence and increasing the risk of conviction on propensity rather than proof of the charged act [S3].

Several provisions are advisory or procedural rather than substantive: the child custody provision is only a 'sense of the Congress' statement with no binding effect on state courts, and the alternative work arrangements subtitle is likewise nonbinding [S2][S3].

The bill's centerpiece harassment remedy requires victims to first use the employer's own grievance procedure, or show it was inappropriate or unreasonably delayed, before recovering the enhanced award — a hurdle that could favor employers with sophisticated internal processes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The civil rights and victim-services core is strong: real money damages and fast injunctive relief for harassment victims, campus crime transparency, funded rape prevention, shelter expansion, and portable protective orders would materially help ordinary people, at a cost mainly to employers who lose harassment cases and to taxpayers through modest grant programs. The bill is most questionable in its criminal and content-liability provisions: suing media sellers for third-party crimes raises serious free-speech problems, the death penalty expansion is a contested response that does nothing to prevent violence, and the broadened admission of prior-offense evidence trades defendant protections for prosecution ease. On balance the public benefit outweighs the cost, but the package is a mix of well-targeted remedies and constitutionally aggressive, punishment-heavy measures.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Senate Minority Leader Robert Dole introduced the bill on February 21, 1991, joined by 13 Republican senators including Simpson, Thurmond, McCain, and D'Amato [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
That referral was the last action of any kind: the action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, no calendar placement, and no floor vote for the remainder of the 102nd Congress [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, killing the bill under the chamber rule that legislation does not carry over between Congresses [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced six-figure harassment penalties and fast-track injunctions kept the existing limited-remedy regime. Producers, distributors, and sellers of sexually explicit material avoided a new wave of civil suits from crime victims. And members of Congress themselves avoided losing their exemption from the employment discrimination law the bill would have extended to Capitol Hill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, adult-media producers, and members of Congress

for.name: Sen. Robert J. Dole
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill as its sponsor on February 21, 1991.

for.name: 13 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Simpson, Thurmond, Cochran, Kasten, Burns, D'Amato, Lugar, McCain, Murkowski, Roth, Seymour, Stevens, and Warner.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action: no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled after the bill's referral on February 21, 1991.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record; all 14 sponsors and cosponsors were Republican, but no documented opposition appears in the record — the bill simply died in committee without a stated opponent.

industries.note: The bill would create monetary penalties up to $100,000–$150,000 for intentional sexual harassment and let victims get immediate court orders, giving harassed workers leverage employers currently do not face. Small employers would get free government technical assistance on compliance, and courts would weigh employer prevention programs in sizing awards.

industries.industry: Producers and distributors of sexually explicit material
industries.note: Crime victims could sue any producer, distributor, exhibitor, or seller of sexually explicit material they could show helped incite a violent sex offense, with damages and attorney's fees. This directly targets the adult media industry's sales of violent or obscene material at the cost of ordinary crime victims' compensation.

Schools would have to collect and publish sexual assault statistics and report them to students, parents, and police — a transparency mandate with compliance costs whose beneficiary is students and families, not the institutions.

industries.industry: Rape crisis centers and domestic violence nonprofits
industries.note: The bill funds rape prevention and education grants, public-awareness campaigns, shelter services including a rural set-aside, and limits law-enforcement training grants to experienced nonprofits — new revenue streams for service providers whose clients are ordinary victims.

industries.industry: Registered apprenticeship programs (building trades and skilled trades)
industries.note: Federal grants and outreach would pay for recruiting and pre-apprenticeship training for women and minorities in registered programs, expanding the pipeline of entrants without mandating anything against the programs.
